content: 1. The use of condoms and vaginal contraceptive diaphragms is not recommended within 72 hours following treatment with clindamycin ovules. 2. Routine treatment of sexual partners is not recommended in cases of bacterial vaginosis (BV). 3. For patients with allergies, intolerance, or adverse reactions to metronidazole or tinidazole, intravaginal clindamycin cream is the preferred treatment. Intravaginal metronidazole gel may be considered for women who are not allergic to metronidazole but cannot tolerate oral administration. Alcohol consumption should be avoided during treatment with nitroimidazoles, and abstinence from alcohol should continue for 24 hours after completing metronidazole or 72 hours after completing tinidazole to reduce the risk of a disulfiram-like reaction. 4. Women with HIV who have bacterial vaginosis should receive the same treatment regimen as those without HIV infection. 5. For Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, individuals who have had sexual contact with an infected patient within the 60 days preceding symptom onset or diagnosis should be referred for evaluation, testing, and presumptive dual treatment. If the last potential sexual exposure occurred more than 60 days before symptom onset or diagnosis, the most recent sexual partner should be treated. To prevent reinfection, sexual partners should abstain from unprotected intercourse for seven days after both they and their partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. 6. In cases of gonococcal meningitis or endocarditis, the preferred treatment regimen is ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 12–24 hours for 10–14 days, combined with a single dose of azithromycin 1 g orally. 7. Mothers of infants with ophthalmia neonatorum caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae should be evaluated, tested, and presumptively treated for gonorrhea, along with their sexual partners. For disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) or scalp abscesses in neonates, the preferred treatment is ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg/day IM/IV once daily for seven days or cefotaxime 25 mg/kg IV/IM every 12 hours for seven days. If meningitis is documented, the treatment duration should be extended to 10–14 days. Ceftriaxone should be used cautiously in hyperbilirubinemic infants, especially those born prematurely. 8. For moderate to severe pneumonia or immunocompromised patients, the preferred regimens include azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 5–7 days or levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 7–10 days (or 750 mg orally once daily for 5–7 days). Alternative regimens include ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily for 14 days, moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 14 days, erythromycin 750–1000 mg IV every 6 hours for 3–7 days followed by 500 mg orally four times daily for a total of 21 days, or clarithromycin 500 mg IV every 12 hours for 3–7 days followed by 500 mg orally twice daily for a total of 21 days. Severely ill patients should receive parenteral therapy until clinical improvement is observed and oral absorption is adequate. 9. For chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, the preferred regimens include azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM in a single dose, ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for three days, or erythromycin base 500 mg orally three times daily for seven days. Patients should be tested for HIV infection at the time of diagnosis, and if initial test results are negative, serologic testing for syphilis and HIV should be repeated three months later. Follow-up should occur 3–7 days after initiating therapy, and ulcers should improve symptomatically within three days and objectively within seven days. If no improvement is observed, clinicians should reassess the diagnosis, consider coinfection with another STD or HIV, evaluate treatment adherence, or investigate antimicrobial resistance. 10. For the first clinical episode of genital herpes, preferred regimens include acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days, acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 7–10 days, valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily for 7–10 days, or famciclovir 250 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days. Treatment can be extended if healing is incomplete after 10 days. 11. For recurrent genital herpes, episodic therapy options include acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for five days, acyclovir 800 mg orally twice daily for five days, acyclovir 800 mg orally three times daily for two days, valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for three days, valacyclovir 1 g orally once daily for five days, famciclovir 125 mg orally twice daily for five days, famciclovir 1 g orally twice daily for one day, or famciclovir 500 mg once followed by 250 mg orally twice daily for two days. 12. For severe HSV disease, acyclovir 5–10 mg/kg IV every eight hours for 2–7 days or until clinical improvement is observed, followed by oral antiviral therapy to complete at least 10 days of total therapy, is recommended. HSV encephalitis requires 21 days of intravenous therapy, and acyclovir dosage should be adjusted for impaired renal function. 13. For neonatal herpes, acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every eight hours is recommended for 14 days if the disease is limited to the skin and mucous membranes or for 21 days for disseminated disease or central nervous system involvement. 14. For acyclovir-resistant genital herpes, preferred regimens include foscarnet 40–80 mg/kg IV every eight hours until clinical resolution. Alternative regimens include cidofovir 5 mg/kg IV once weekly or topical imiquimod applied to lesions once daily for five consecutive days. 15. For trichomoniasis in adults, the preferred regimens are metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose. An alternative regimen is metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for seven days. Pregnant women should be treated with metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose, and breastfeeding should be avoided for 12–24 hours after metronidazole or 72 hours after tinidazole. 16. For uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is recommended. Artemether-lumefantrine is a preferred regimen, with doses ideally spaced eight hours apart for the first two doses. For chloroquine-sensitive Plasmodium vivax malaria, chloroquine is the preferred treatment, given as a total dose of 25 mg/kg over three days. For chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium vivax, ACTs containing piperaquine, mefloquine, or lumefantrine are recommended. 17. For liver stages (hypnozoites) of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, a 14-day course of primaquine is recommended to prevent relapse, except in pregnant women, infants under six months, breastfeeding women with infants under six months, or individuals with G6PD deficiency.
